title: All of a kind vs. mixed in kind
core: Every word here judges how alike the members of a set are — whether a group is all one thing or a mix of unlike things. The trap is that they answer different questions: some describe what a whole is *made of*, some claim one member can *replace* another, some assert a *parallel* between things known to differ, and some deliver a *verdict* on the mixture rather than a description of it. Two also smuggle in extra freight — a shared starting point, or a claim of total coverage — that has nothing to do with likeness. Sort by which question the sentence is actually asking before you pick.

words.nuance: The baseline sameness word, and it is about **composition** only: what the whole is made of, part by part. It never claims the parts can substitute for one another or serve the same purpose — a **homogeneous** sample is uniform in makeup, full stop.

The strictest and narrowest: units are so identical *for accounting purposes* that which one you receive is not a question anyone can ask. Contractual and financial in origin — **fungible** things are counted, not compared, which is why applying it to people reads as brutal.

The claim is functional, not compositional: two things may differ in material, brand, or wording and still be **interchangeable** if swapping them changes no outcome. Unlike *fungible*, they need not be the same kind of unit — only equal in effect.

The outlier: it concedes the two things are unalike in substance and asserts only that the *relation* between them matches. **Analogous** is an argumentative move — it licenses reasoning from one case to the other — and it always takes *to*, which the sameness words never do.

Not about likeness at all but about **scope**: it says a claim covers every case with zero exceptions. A **universal** group can be wildly mixed internally; what is uniform is the applicability, and one counterexample destroys the claim.

The flat technical antonym of *homogeneous* — same axis (composition), opposite value, same absence of praise. It usually flags a practical obstacle: **heterogeneous** data won't pool, **heterogeneous** results mean the studies disagree.

Escalates unlikeness into **incomparability**: the differences are of kind, so grouping or comparing the items is illegitimate. Where *heterogeneous* merely records a mix, **disparate** objects to it — it is the word used to reject an analogy.

The only one that requires a **shared origin** and a time dimension: things diverge because they began together and the gap widened. It describes a trajectory, not a composition — and it measures the angle coolly, without the condemnation of *deviant*.

The mix plus a **curator**: someone chose across boundaries on merit, so the variety is credited to taste. It is the one approving word here — and it quietly denies originality, since an **eclectic** thinker borrows rather than invents.

The only **noun**, and the only outright insult: the mixture is incoherent because nobody planned it. It is *eclectic* with the curator removed — informal, lightly contemptuous, and it implies the thing should be scrapped and rebuilt.

exam_note: The exam plants *analogous* and *universal* in sameness contexts where they don't fit — neither describes a mixture — and forces the *homogeneous / fungible / interchangeable* choice on a single hinge: made of the same stuff, countable as equal units, or equal in effect.
